title: Two ‘forever chemicals’ associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in NIH analysis
text:
Two ‘forever chemicals’ associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in NIH analysis
Thursday, November 5, 2026
Evidence continues to grow on how environmental factors affect women’s health.
Women with higher blood levels of two common per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also familiarly known as PFAS, were more likely to develop estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer, according to a new study by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). PFAS are a large group of chemicals used in common consumer products. Often referred to as “forever chemicals,” PFAS do not break down easily in the environment and can remain in the body for years.
The study found that women with higher blood plasma levels of two of these substances, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), were associated with a higher incidence of ER-negative breast cancer. No clear association was observed between the two chemicals and breast cancer risk overall.
“Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump’s leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.”
ER-negative tumors lack receptors that allow hormone estrogen to help cancer cells grow. Compared with breast cancers that respond to hormone estrogen, ER-negative breast cancers tend to be more aggressive and have worse outcomes. Scientists know less about what raises the risk of this type of breast cancer.
“Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors,” explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study. The findings are reported in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.
NIH researchers and their collaborators measured 17 PFAS in blood, collected years before women were diagnosed with cancer. Women in the group with the highest PFOA levels had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than those in the lowest group. For PFOS, the rate was 93% higher, or nearly twice as high. These numbers describe relative differences between groups, not an individual woman’s chance of getting breast cancer.
The research drew on the Sister Study, led by NIH’s National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). The larger study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35–74 in the United States and Puerto Rico from 2003 to 2009. None had breast cancer when they joined the Sister Study, but each had a full or half-sister who had been previously diagnosed with breast cancer. For the PFAS study, researchers included 1,609 women who developed breast cancer and a comparison sample of 2,269 women.
“These findings matter for women’s health broadly,” said first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., a former research fellow at NIH and a current researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. “Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention.”
Because the strongest associations involved tumors without hormone receptors, the authors suggest that PFAS may affect cancer risk through other non-hormonal biologic pathways. Possible pathways include changes in gene activity or immune system. However, this study did not test those explanations. The authors say future studies should evaluate people with higher PFAS exposure and in groups more affected by ER-negative breast cancer.
Although most individuals have measurable levels of PFOA and PFOS in their bodies, these compounds have been largely phased out and replaced with new PFAS compounds. “More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals,” White said.
This research was supported by NIEHS grants: Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.

title: First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
text:
First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
November 5, 2026 10:00 AM ET Heard on Morning Edition Jennifer Ludden
The share of first-time homebuyers remains at a near-record low of 22% as a housing shortage and high prices sideline many, according to a new report by the National Association of Realtors. But those who are managing to buy are older and wealthier than in the past, and 1 in 10 paid all cash, a record high since such data was collected starting in 2003.
"Inheritances are really driving this," said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at the NAR.
First-time buyers who paid all-cash were more likely than those who financed a house to use an inheritance (28%) or proceeds from the sale of an inherited property (21%). They were also older.
NAR finds the median age of all first-time buyers remains at 40, a record high. For first-time buyers who financed a purchase it was 38, while for those who paid all-cash it was 54. "They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come through," Lautz said.
For first-time buyers overall, personal savings was the biggest source of funding for a down payment. But in another shift, more people used assets – like a 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency – than financial help from family or friends. Older buyers have had more time to save up, Lautz said, but she thinks there's another factor: "I think it's uncomfortable to ask mom and dad for a gift or loan when you're hitting 40 versus your young 30s."
The share of first time buyers using an inheritance is likely to grow in coming years as boomers reach their 80's and beyond. As the report noted, "there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth."
Real estate agents around the country are seeing the change.
"I would say in the first 15 years of my career, I saw virtually zero first-time home buyers paying all cash," said Jason Miller, a broker with Trust Real Estate Company in St. Cloud, Minn.
But he's had a number of them since the COVID-19 pandemic, when homebuying surged. "They knew they had to absolutely have the most sterling offer possible to compete in the competitive marketplace," he said.
High mortgage rates are also driving all-cash bids, Miller said, since they make it far more expensive to finance a home for 30 years. And not all families wait until death to pass on wealth. Miller sees more clients getting help from family members who may have paid off their own home, or have equity in a second property they can sell and "are gifting some or all of that money." They're viewing it as a kind of "future inheritance," he said.
For some younger first-time buyers, relatives may only be "lending them the cash" to make a bid more attractive, said Nate Johnson, a broker associate with RedKey Realty Leaders in St. Louis. Even with much of the national housing market in a major slump, he said his local market is still intensely competitive for buyers.
"They just know that if we're looking at five or six offers on the table, let's call it 10 offers on the table, which is not uncommon…maybe three of those offers will be all cash," he said.
After closing on a property, Johnson has seen some buyers refinance into a mortgage and pay back their family member.
The rise of all-cash offers makes the market even tougher for those who struggle to save up for a down payment with today's sky-high home prices.
"For a long time I thought I wanted to buy a house," said Seth Daphne Esmeson, who lives in Seattle and will soon turn 33. They and their spouse have good jobs, but also debt, including a car payment and student loans. Not only does Esmeson think they may never be in a position to buy, they've also decided it does not make sense at today's prices.
"Being that debt burdened, and also having to fix things on your home, like, it sounds really terrible," they said.
Esmeson is also not convinced that home equity would outpace other investments. They like their current rental and landlord so are sticking with it for now.
Still, it's frustrating that the housing market worked better for previous generations. "We have the short end of the deal," they said, and "the gap is expanding."
There's probably only one way they might ever be able to buy. "If I received an inheritance," they said. But "I love my mom dearly and I don't want to look forward to that, or really want to strategize around that."

title: Rubio says there's 'zero' information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor
text:
Rubio says there's 'zero' information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor
November 18, 2026 3:27 AM ET By The Associated Press
MANILA, Philippines — Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's "zero" information that the cascade of service outages, which snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications, are related to each other or to a malign actor.
Rubio sought to calm Americans as he traveled with President Donald Trump and they prepared to leave the Philippines for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the tech hub of Shenzhen, China.
"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.
In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for disruptions — and even staunch Trump allies have accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause.
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage on Tuesday.
"It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine," Trump said in Manila, declaring that "things like that happen."
But as concern mounted, Rubio appeared to publicly address American worries from the other side of the world.
There has been a steady stream of outages this week
Trump's nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages was an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.
The series of outages began Thursday, when Microsoft's email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to "an earlier network capacity upgrade."
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by "a software bug" and was "not cyber-related."
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as "routine maintenance."
Trump's nonchalance was not shared by some of his allies
Earlier Tuesday, Karoline Leavitt, Trump's former press secretary, said the White House needed to do more to explain the situation.
"What I would say to the White House is: transparency is key," Leavitt said on Fox News. Later on social media, she praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network.
"Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyberattack incident," Clayton said, explaining that the U.S. government believes the incidents were caused by security upgrades that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump's Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical of the lack of information from the federal government.
"Americans aren't stupid," she posted on social media. "We want and deserve to know what's really going on."
Meghan McCain, a conservative commentator who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, voiced similar concerns.
"Someone high in the administration needs to get on TV and tell the American people NOW what is going on," McCain, who is also the daughter of late GOP Sen. John McCain, wrote on X. "No one who lived through COVID is believing this is all a coincidence."
After Trump and other administration officials failed to offer reassurance on those cascading tech problems, Rubio seemed to take on the role of reassurer-in-chief when he appeared unexpectedly in Manila to take questions. The secretary of state is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, though he lately has declined to comment on whether he would consider a campaign to try to succeed Trump.
But Trump's role in the immediate moment was a pressing concern, even for supporters in his Make America Great Again movement.
"Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyberattack," Laura Loomer, a right-wing personality known for her incendiary social media presence, wrote on X. "President Trump should come back to the United States." She did not present any evidence of an attack.
Conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer, writing on X, demanded accountability. "And why does it feel like we're being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?" she said.
